Its elevation must be set at such an inclination that it corresponds to the <term>Pythagorean right-angled triangle</term> <gloss>a geometric principle where the sides are in a 3:4:5 ratio</gloss>. This means the length should be divided into five parts; the head of the screw is raised by three of these parts, so that the distance from the perpendicular to the lower end is four parts. The method of how this should be arranged at the extremity is described in the form <note>or diagram</note> at the end of the book.

<margin>
a. A screw erected according to the ratio of a Pythagorean triangle.
b. The beam in which the screw rotates.
</margin>

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts an Archimedean screw used for irrigation or drainage. The device consists of a wooden shaft with an internal spiral encased in a cylinder, tilted at an angle. The lower end is submerged in water, and the upper end is supported by a tall wooden pillar (labeled 'b'). A large treadwheel (labeled 'd') is attached to the center of the shaft, allowing humans to turn the device by treading on its rungs. Water is shown being lifted through the screw and discharging from the top into a wooden trough or basin. The letter 'a' labels the main body of the screw.</note>

Regarding the material from which machines are made for drawing water, the methods by which they are completed, and the means by which, receiving motion, they provide rotations for endless utilities,

<summary>This page concludes the technical description of the Archimedean screw by specifying the ideal angle of inclination based on a 3:4:5 right triangle and introduces the broader subject of water-lifting machines.</summary>
<keywords>Archimedean screw, Pythagorean triangle, hydraulic machines, water lifting, engineering, Vitruvius</keywords>
